<em>Room to Respond</em>. Pick countries from the map or the search box, choose an
index, and set the year range to compare them over time.</p>

<div class="ps-notes rule-top">
  <p class="mono eyebrow">How the indices are built, and what they cannot see</p>

  <p><strong>Policy Buffers Index (PBI).</strong> An equal-weighted average of six observable
  components: the inverse debt ratio, the fiscal balance, the real policy rate, the current
  account balance, foreign reserves over GDP, and the inverse long-rate spread over the United
  States as a market-access measure. Each is signed so higher means more room, converted to a
  within-year percentile rank before averaging. No estimation is involved, so anyone can audit
  it.</p>

  <p><strong>Effective Space Index (ESI).</strong> The within-year percentile rank of an
  effective-space measure predicted by a random forest fitted to crisis outcomes over a wider
  state vector. It changes both the recipe and the ingredients relative to the PBI.</p>

  <p class="ps-caveat-h">Caveats that bear directly on how these charts should be read</p>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Uneven coverage.</strong> A country is ranked once it reports four of the six
    components, so economies with sparse statistics can be ranked on partial information. The
    spread component in particular is missing for much of the sample.</li>

    <li><strong>The indices reward what is measured.</strong> Large reported reserve stocks and
    fiscal surpluses lift commodity exporters. Capacities that no input measures — reserve
    currency status, swap lines, deep local investor bases, institutional strength — count for
    nothing, which mechanically favours some countries over others.</li>

    <li><strong>Neighbouring ranks are not meaningful distinctions.</strong> Inputs arrive with
    error and reporting lags that are largest outside advanced economies.</li>

    <li><strong>The ESI is noisy, and its country-level calls deserve skepticism.</strong> The
    average 68 percent interval on a 2019 score spans 7.9 log points against a cross-country
    interquartile range of 3.6, so within-year ordering is dominated by estimation error.
    Year-to-year rank persistence is 0.72, against 0.83 for the buffers index. The paper
    presents it as an informative companion to the PBI, not a validated ranking and not a
    replacement.</li>

    <li><strong>ESI rankings are specification-sensitive.</strong> The United States sits 122nd
    of 154 on the 2019 cross section, but between 70th and 122nd across the forest
    configurations examined.</li>

    <li><strong>Two known failures are deliberate exhibits.</strong> Russia sits in the top
    tenth on low debt and a large reserve stock, while the sanctions regime in place since 2014
    already constrained exactly the market access an effective measure ought to capture. The
    United States sits 139th of 144 on the PBI, which is mechanically correct yet hard to
    credit for the issuer of the world's reserve currency — it pairs a bottom-decile debt score
    and persistent deficits with a measured reserve stock near zero relative to GDP, because a
    country whose currency others hold as reserves has little need to hold reserves itself.</li>

    <li><strong>Scores are within-year percentiles.</strong> A country can rise because others
    fell. Levels are not comparable to any absolute standard, and a score is a position in a
    distribution, not a quantity of fiscal space.</li>
  </ul>

  <p class="ps-src">Source: author's calculations, from <em>Room to Respond</em>.
  Country outlines from Natural Earth (public domain); boundaries and names do not imply any
  judgement on the legal status of any territory. Northern Cyprus, Somaliland and Kosovo are
  absent from the basemap as they carry no ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 code.</p>
